runApp("final_app", display.mode = "showcase")

# Movie dataset

This dataset is taken from the package `ggplot2movies`.

[link to the description
online](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/doc/ggplot2movies/movies.html)

## The data

There are various ways to use the data from this package. We can load it
as `ggplot2movies::movies`, however, this does not store it as a
variable in our environment. So, we can assign it to a variable or we
can load it using `data` to store it as a variable.

```{r store data as an object, include = FALSE}
movies <- ggplot2movies::movies
```

## Simple data exploration

```{r initial exploration, echo = TRUE}
head(movies)
dim(movies)
glimpse(movies)
class(movies)
```

## Summary statistics

In the following table, basic statistics for the relevant numerical
variables in the dataset are summarised

```{r}
movies |> 
  select(2:6) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable", 
               values_to ="value") |>
  group_by(variable) |> 
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Minimum = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Maximum = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Missing = sum(is.na(value))) 

```

The data contains:

- 58,788 movies (rows)

- 24 columns:

  - Movie title
  - Year
  - Length (minutes)
  - Budget
  - Rating
  - Votes
  - r1-10 (percentile per score 1-10, rounded to nearest 10%)
  - MPAA rating
  - Genre (action, animation, comedy, drama, documentary, romance,
    short)

## Data tidying and transformation

We tidy the data by:

- trimming whitespaces

- saving as a tibble

- eliminating the variables "budget" and "mpaa". These contain many
  `NAs` and empty characters, which is why we did not consider them.

- making sure all numeric variables were considered as numeric

- introducing the possibility of filtering movies that have votes higher
  than a certain cutoff

- introducing a column "decade" classifying movies into their decade

- introducing a column "genre" summarising the data from the separate
  genre columns

```{r transform the data }
# we wanted to be able to change the cutoff later on, but ended up including it as an option in our shiny app instead
cutoff_votes <- 0

# genre assignment with accounting for multiple assignments per movie instead of labelling them as crosslisted
genres <- c("Action", "Animation", "Comedy", "Drama", "Documentary", "Romance")


#Create a new clean dataset
clean_movies <- movies |>   
  map(~str_trim(.x)) |>   
  as_tibble() |> 
  select(-budget, -mpaa) |> 
  mutate_at(vars(-title), as.numeric) |>
  mutate(genre = factor(case_when(rowSums(pick(Action:Romance)) > 1 ~ "Crosslisted",
                                  Action == 1 ~ "Action",
                                  Animation == 1 ~ "Animation",
                                  Comedy == 1 ~ "Comedy",
                                  Drama == 1 ~ "Drama",
                                  Documentary == 1 ~ "Documentary",
                                  Romance == 1 ~ "Romance",
                                  rowSums(pick(Action:Romance)) < 1 ~ "No genre"))) |> 
  filter(votes >= cutoff_votes)|> 
  mutate(decade = if_else(year %in% seq(2000,2005, 1),
                          paste0(year  %/% 10 * 10),
                  if_else(year %in% seq(1900, 1909, 1),
                          paste0("190",(year - 1900) %/% 10 * 10), 
                  if_else(year %in% seq(1910, 1999, 1),
                          paste0("19",(year - 1900) %/% 10 * 10), 
                          # introducing decade column
                          "1890")))) |> arrange (year) |> 
  mutate_at(vars(decade), as.numeric) |>
  mutate(genre_combo = apply(
         pick(all_of(genres)), 1,
         \(x) paste(genres[as.logical(x)], collapse = " + ")
       ),
       genre_combo = factor(ifelse(genre_combo == "", "None", genre_combo))
)


#Save clean datasets 
saveRDS(clean_movies, "final_app/data/clean_movies.rds")
saveRDS(clean_movies, "clean_movies.rds")
```

# Analysis

We focus on exploring the different variables of our dataset
individually and testing whether they can predict the rating of a movie.

First, some exploration of highest and lowest rated movies, also in our
shiny.

## Highest and lowest rated movies

*Here we consider all the genre combinations, but we made it simpler in
the final app*

```{r}
vote_cutoff = 1000

# finding the highest and lowest rated movies on IMDB and their statistics
highest_table <- clean_movies |> 
  filter(votes >= vote_cutoff) |>
  filter(rating == max(rating)) |>
  select(title, year, rating, votes, genre_combo, length) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = str_glue("Highest rated of movies with more than {vote_cutoff} votes on IMDB")) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    year  = "Year",
    rating = "Rating (1-10)",
    votes = "Votes",
    genre_combo = "Genre(s)",
    length = "Length (min)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = votes, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = rating, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) |>
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Data from ggplot2's movies dataset.",
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  )

highest_table

lowest_table <- clean_movies |> 
  filter(votes > vote_cutoff) |>
  filter(rating == min(rating)) |>
  select(title, year, rating, votes, genre_combo, length) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = str_glue("Lowest rated of movies with more than {vote_cutoff} votes on IMDB")) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    year  = "Year",
    rating = "Rating (1-10)",
    votes = "Votes",
    genre_combo = "Genre(s)",
    length = "Length (min)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = votes, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = rating, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) |>
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Data from ggplot2's movies dataset.",
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  )

lowest_table
```

## Temporal

*Attempted to analyse the data based on the decades. Later decided to
focus on the years, as we incorporated a slider into the shiny plot and
knew that specific decades could still be selected that way.*

```{r}
#Datasets used for plotting of the variable year
mean_ratings_decade <- clean_movies |> 
  group_by(decade) |>  
  mutate(mean_rating_decade = mean(rating))  |>  tally(name = "number of movies") 

mean_ratings_decade

saveRDS(mean_ratings_decade, "final_app/data/movies_per_decade.rds")
```

## Overview Table by Genre

```{r genre table}
table(factor(clean_movies$genre))  # basic table with number of movies per genre

genre_table <- clean_movies |>
  filter(votes > 20) |>
  group_by(genre_combo) |> # either put in genre or genre_combo
  summarise(
    n_movies     = n(),
    n_votes      = sum(votes),
    avg_rating   = mean(rating),
    wtd_rating   = sum(votes * rating) / n_votes) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Genre representation of movies on IMDB"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    genre_combo       = "Genre / genre combination",
    n_movies    = "Number of movies",
    n_votes     = "Total number of votes",
    avg_rating  = "Average rating",
    wtd_rating  = "Vote-weighted rating" # those movies with more votes have higher influence on average
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(n_movies, n_votes),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(avg_rating, wtd_rating),
    decimals = 1
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) |>
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Data from ggplot2's movies dataset.",
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  )

genre_table

# code for table with the help of rbloggers to make it pretty: https://www.r-bloggers.com/2024/10/table-it-like-a-pro-print-ready-tables-in-r/
```

## Data distributions

The distribution of each relevant numerical variable can be visualized
in the following density graphs. These are: year, length, rating, and
number of votes.

```{r}
clean_movies |> 
  pivot_longer(
  cols = c(year, length, rating, votes),   
  names_to = "variable",      
  values_to = "value"         
) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = variable, colour = variable)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ variable, 
    scales = "free",
  labeller = as_labeller(c(
    "year" = "Year",
    "length"= "Length",
    "rating"= "Rating",
    "votes"= "Number of votes"))) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

## General data visualizations

### Visualize rating patterns in the top 20 movies

We consider the 20 movies with the highest average rating and plot in a
heatmap the percentage of votes awarding 1-10 ratings.

This visualizes that, although these movies are equally highly rated,
there are differences in the percentage of each score that can be
assigned by users. For example, most have a 100% of 10/10 votes, while
movie "The phantom submarine" has a more heterogeneous distribution of
scores.

```{r}
top_movies_rating <- clean_movies |> 
  select(title, rating, r1:r10) |> 
  arrange(desc(rating)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 20)

matrix_rating <- as.matrix(top_movies_rating |> select(r1:r10))
rownames(matrix_rating) <- top_movies_rating$title

heatmap_rating <- superheat(
  matrix_rating,, 
  pretty.order.rows = TRUE,
  heat.col.scheme = "viridis",
  grid.hline.col = "white",
  grid.vline.col = "white",
  left.label.col = c("lightpink1", "white"),
  bottom.label.col =c("lightpink1", "white"),
  left.label.text.size = 2.5,
  bottom.label.text.angle = 0
)
```
